extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and policymakers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (originally: the people of New York); readers interested in constitutional interpretation and federal-state taxation powers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the standards and interpretive rules Hamilton (Publius) advances about the allocation and exercise of taxation powers under the proposed U.S. Constitution, including when powers are exclusive, concurrent, and how to read clauses like 'necessary and proper' and the Supremacy Clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive delegation of State sovereignty (three cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: State sovereignty is only exclusively alienated to the Union in three cases: (1) where the Constitution in express terms granted an exclusive authority to the Union; (2) where it granted in one instance an authority to the Union and in another prohibited the States from exercising the like authority; and (3) where it granted an authority to the Union to which a similar authority in the States would be absolutely and totally contradictory and repugnant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: (1) 'exclusive legislation' over the federal district; (2) power to lay and collect duties on imports combined with the prohibition on states laying imposts/duties on imports/exports (yielding exclusivity for duties on imports); (3) uniform rule of naturalization (if states could prescribe distinct rules, uniformity impossible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent taxation authority (all other taxes except import/export duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to impose taxes on all articles other than exports and imports is a concurrent and coequal authority in the United States and in the individual States; there is no expression making that power exclusive in the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: the restriction on states with respect to import/export duties (Article I, §10) implies their authority as to other taxes; absent explicit divestment, states retain taxing authority. Practical consequences and mutual prudence govern overlapping impositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative pregnant as an interpretive clue
rubrics_metrics.description: A prohibitory clause (e.g., forbidding states to lay duties on imports/exports) functions as a 'negative pregnant'—a negation of one thing and an affirmation of another—implying the states' authority to tax other articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues it would be sophistry to read the prohibition as implying that states could only tax other articles 'subject to the control of the national legislature'; instead, the restriction implies an affirmative concurrent power for states over other taxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and Proper clause is declaratory of means, not a new power
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause authorizing Congress to make all laws which shall be 'necessary and proper' for carrying into execution the powers vested by the Constitution is largely declaratory: a power to do X implies the power to employ the means necessary to do X; the clause merely states that truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to taxation: a power to lay and collect taxes inevitably includes the power to pass laws necessary and proper to execute that power. If any objection exists, it must be to the specific substantive powers, not to the general declaratory clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy Clause limited to laws 'made in pursuance' of the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution, federal laws made 'in pursuance thereof,' and treaties 'the supreme law of the land,' but this supremacy extends only to laws made pursuant to the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts of the Union not pursuant to constitutional powers are usurpations and do not become supreme law. The clause is thus a declaratory limitation and a guard against misreading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who judges necessity and propriety (initial and ultimate adjudication)
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government must, in the first instance, judge of the proper exercise of its powers; the people (constituents) judge in the last instance and must appeal and take measures to redress overreaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the federal legislature exceeds jurisdiction (e.g., varying a State's law of descent or abrogating a state's land tax), it is evident as overreach and the people must remedy it; practical political remedies and constitutional standards guide correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repugnancy test for implied exclusion of state power
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied exclusion of state authority requires an immediate constitutional repugnancy between a federal grant and a state power; mere possibility of inconvenience, imprudence, or policy conflict does not extinguish pre-existing state sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A state tax that makes further federal taxation inexpedient is a matter of prudence, not constitutional impotence. Only a direct contradiction of authority will imply exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residuary authorities remain with States unless explicitly divested
rubrics_metrics.description: All authorities of which the States are not explicitly divested in favor of the Union remain with them in full vigor; the instrument's negative clauses (e.g., Article I §10) indicate the Convention's intent and furnish an interpretive rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general rule of interpretation: read the constitution as a whole and rely on explicit negative clauses to identify where state powers were meant to be curtailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy/financial consequences of restricting federal taxation to few objects
rubrics_metrics.description: If federal taxation were confined to particular objects (e.g., only duties on imports), two evils would result: oppression of particular branches of industry and unequal distribution of taxes among states and citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exorbitant import duties would encourage smuggling, prejudice fair traders, create premature monopolies for manufacturers, and often fall upon merchants rather than consumers; thus design of revenue sources must consider economic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal fiscal needs justify broad, indefinite capacity to tax
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal expenditures (defense, wars, national debt) are potentially unlimited and require a capacity to provide for future contingencies; state expenditures are comparatively limited, so the Union must have broad taxing capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: support of navy and armies, payment of war debts; comparison to Great Britain's budgetary proportions and to past U.S. war debts. Constitutions should provide for probable contingencies, not solely present needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction as the practical constitutional compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: A concurrent jurisdiction in taxation was 'the only admissible substitute' for total subordination of state authority; it reconciles an indefinite federal taxing power with an adequate and independent power in the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrent jurisdiction allows the Union sufficient resources for national purposes while preserving states' ability to supply local needs; any separation of objects of revenue would sacrifice national interests to state power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the instrument's structure and explicit prohibitions as interpretive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of grants of power should account for the constitution's explicit negative restrictions and structure; these internal provisions are evidence of the Convention's practical sense about the proper allocation of powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tenth Section of the First Article (negative prohibitions on state powers) is cited as a clear indicator of the Convention's intent, serving as a rule of interpretation for residuary state authorities.
